CHAPTER 7: KEY ARGUMENTS CONCERNING REPRESENTATION

LEARNING OUTCOMES
- 2.4 Arguments concerning representation: identify which ideas and arguments from Topics 1.2 and 1.3 are relevant at national level.
- 2.5 Evidence about the effectiveness of representation: summarise evidence on how well the Irish electoral system represents the will of all Irish people; engage with different viewpoints and use evidence to reach a conclusion; evaluate a piece of qualitative or quantitative research on representation, commenting on the quality of the evidence and conclusions.
- In Chapter 3 these arguments were applied to the school system; now they are applied at national level.
- Links to culture, identity, the political system, gender and human rights.

7.1 KEY ARGUMENTS CONCERNING REPRESENTATION (from Topics 1.2 and 1.3)
- Those with the most power or influence can make rules that suit their own interests, not everyone's.
- Rules protect weaker members of the community from stronger members.
- Those with the most knowledge and wisdom should play the strongest role in making rules.
- There is a danger of those with power enforcing rules arbitrarily.
- There should be very few rules, only to keep people safe; more than that infringes freedom.
- It is compliance with norms and values, not enforcement of rules, that keeps order.

DIMENSIONS OF POWER (applied at national level)
- 1. Getting people to act in ways they would not otherwise act.
- 2. Being able to set rules or practices that benefit some groups over others.
- 3. Shaping ideas so people think one way of doing things is the best or only way (ideology).
- 4. Power exercised by a range of people or groups, including those who seem institutionally 'powerless'.

CASE STUDY: DIRECT PROVISION IN IRELAND
KEY TERMS
- Direct Provision: the basic level of food and shelter for asylum seekers in Ireland while their refugee status is processed (instead of cash payments, according to Gov.ie).
- Asylum seeker: a person seeking international protection whose claim has not yet been decided. Not every asylum seeker becomes a refugee, but every refugee is first an asylum seeker.
- Refugee: a person who has fled their country and is unwilling or unable to return because of fear of persecution due to nationality, religion, race, or membership of a social or political group.
- Economic migrant: someone who leaves their country purely for financial or economic reasons, to find a better life; not fleeing persecution, so not entitled to international protection.
- Resettlement: refugees transferred from the country where they sought refuge to another state that agrees to admit them; usually given long-term residence or asylum and a chance of citizenship.
- Stateless person: a person who, under national laws, has no legal bond of nationality with any state.
- Profit: most Direct Provision systems are run by private contractors on a for-profit basis.

HOW DIRECT PROVISION WORKS (according to Amnesty International)
- Began on 10 April 2000 (introduced in 1999, in service from 2000).
- Asylum seeker applies on arrival; stays first in a reception centre in Dublin; then assigned to one of 47 regional Direct Provision Centres.
- Gets three meals a day, a place to sleep and a weekly allowance: €38.80 per adult and €29.80 per child.
- Help with clothing or emergency needs; free medical care in the centre.
- Can apply to access the job market nine months after lodging the application.
- Children aged 4-16 go to local schools. University is usually not free for asylum seekers.
- IGEES (Irish Government Economic and Evaluation Service): Direct Provision 'encompasses a range of State services, including accommodation, food, health and education' provided through government departments and agencies.
- Originally an emergency, short-term measure, mainly for people fleeing the Balkan war. It became long-term; people kept in centres for years say it infringes their human rights.
- Centres are often in B&Bs, hostels, private housing, caravan parks and temporary shelters. Whole families often share a single room with no cooking facilities; residents lose basic choices about how to live.
- McMahon Report (commissioned 2017): accommodation not up to standard, so more money spent on upgrades, raising costs.
- In 2020 the State spent more than €175 million on Direct Provision. Costs rising due to more asylum seekers and longer processing.

KEY ISSUES WITH DIRECT PROVISION
- Employment: no right to work until February 2018; restrictions remain, so most residents have no access to employment.
- Education: limited access to further and higher education.
- Children: children born into the system make up 30% of residents; long-term effects on development unknown.
- Standards and monitoring: conditions vary between centres; inspections focus on health and safety, not emotional or social needs.
- Length of time: average stay 24 months; some residents up to 12 years.

ENDING DIRECT PROVISION
- Government had planned to end Direct Provision by 2024.
- White Paper (a government policy document offering solutions to an issue) on ending Direct Provision published February 2021 by the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth - move to a not-for-profit system in two phases.
- Phase One: four-month stay in a state-owned centre (six centres in total); orientation programme including English classes; bank accounts set up and Irish driving licences for those who can drive; early access to legal aid and healthcare; daily expenses allowance until Phase Two.
- Phase Two: self-contained own-door apartments (houses for families) in the community; NGOs support vulnerable people; access to education and health; further English supports; income support such as the Welfare Allowance; child support payments; access to employment and help finding work.

KEY DEBATE AND THINKERS FOR DIRECT PROVISION
- Is Direct Provision an example of people in power exerting control over the powerless? How is the Government exercising power over asylum seekers?
- Thinkers to apply: Thomas Hobbes (power); Robert Nozick (minimal state); Karl Marx (oppression and struggle of the powerless); Samuel Huntington (clash of civilisations and identity); John Locke (power and rights); John Rawls (veil of ignorance); Edward Said (orientalism and identity); Paulo Freire (oppression); Kwame Anthony Appiah (cosmopolitanism).
- Case study also useful for human rights and identity topics.

7.2 IS OUR ELECTORAL SYSTEM REPRESENTATIVE? DOES IT NEED REFORM?
- You must justify your view with quantitative and qualitative data (see Chapter 4).
- Topics to explore:
- 1. Our electoral system: Ireland uses indirect democracy - is it the best or most effective?
- 2. The voting system: PRSTV compared to First Past The Post and the D'Hondt system.
- 3. Parish-Pump Politics and the dominance of the Healy-Rae family in Kerry.
- 4. Effectiveness of the Houses of the Oireachtas, especially the Seanad.
- 5. The President as a check and balance (or mere symbolism?).
- 6. The Citizens' Assembly amplifying the voice of the people.
- 7. Women and representation in government.
- 8. Minority communities - are they excluded? (LGBTQ+ community, Travelling Community, people in Direct Provision, Irish citizens under 18 who cannot vote.)

THE CITIZENS' ASSEMBLY
- Citizens' Assembly: a randomly selected group of people who deliberate on important issues affecting society.
- Brings citizens together to discuss important policy and legal issues; makes recommendations and reports back to the Oireachtas.
- Members chosen at random from the electoral register, to reflect Irish society by gender, age, region and social class.
- Each assembly agrees its own procedures; can invite and accept submissions from interested people.
- Develops draft recommendations and votes on each, then recommends to the Houses of the Oireachtas. Government responds and arranges Oireachtas debates.
- 2023 Citizens' Assembly on drug use. Issues: drivers, attitudes, trends and prevalence of drug use; harmful impacts on families, communities and individuals; best practice in rehabilitation and recovery; opportunities and challenges of reforming law, policy and operational response (justice, health, education).
- Other assemblies: gender equality (2021) and loss of biodiversity.
- Questions: does it strengthen democracy? Is it just a 'talk tank'? Can it hold governments to account, amplify people's voices, bring major change? Does it enhance or inhibit representation?

WOMEN AND REPRESENTATION
- Gender quota: a target number of women to be reached so more women are represented in government and decision-making.
- 2012: Oireachtas law requires parties to run at least 30% female and at least 30% male candidates in general elections.
- Effect: women elected rose from 16% (2011) to 22% (2016). By 2020, 22.5% - Ireland 98th in the world for women in national parliaments, behind Iraq and China.
- 2016: 35 women elected to the Dáil, more than ever, but only 22% of TDs.
- 2021 Citizens' Assembly recommended: by end of 2022 extend quotas to European, Seanad and local elections; increase penalties for parties that miss the quota; raise the threshold to 40% for both men and women.
- National Women's Council of Ireland: women must be represented at all levels; women furthest from power (low-income, Traveller, LGBTQ+, disabled women) feel the impact of policy most and face extra barriers, so targets and quotas are needed.
- For gender quotas: more women elected, more representation; young women can see women in government and aspire to it; a temporary solution to a patriarchal society.
- Against gender quotas: 'indirect discrimination' - a better man may lose out so the quota is filled; women's work may be branded 'tokenistic' or undeserved; society has moved away from patriarchy, so women have equal opportunity without quotas.
- Links to gender and patriarchy (Chapter 8).

MINORITY AND UNDER-REPRESENTED GROUPS
- Decide whether minority communities are under-represented because of how we elect politicians: e.g. LGBTQ+, Travelling Community, people in Direct Provision.
- Can be approached from a social class view: is the electoral system elitist, favouring the privileged?
- Young people (Chapter 2 - student voice) are excluded as under-18s cannot vote.
- Research prompts: percentage of population (CSO data), protests, organisations that help them, areas of under-representation, what government could do (Citizens' Assembly, education, social contract).

EXAM PRACTICE
- HL short: one argument for and one against gender quotas (2019, 5 marks); name a minority community and how it is discriminated against; is our social contract protecting everyone?
- HL essay (2019, 100 marks): 'As we celebrate 100 years of Dáil Éireann, discuss whether the Irish electoral system is in need of reform' - consider PRSTV, coalitions, representation by gender and background. Use contemporary evidence and at least two Key Thinkers (one named on the course).
- OL: strategies to increase women's participation; meaningful consultation; qualitative vs quantitative census data on Travellers.

rows.prompt: Which is one of the key arguments concerning representation?
options: Rules protect weaker members from stronger members
Rules should always be set by the oldest citizens
Rules are only needed during elections
Rules should be set by private companies
rows.explanation: One key argument is that rules protect weaker members of the community from stronger ones.

rows.prompt: Shaping ideas so people see one way as the only way is which dimension of power?
rows.explanation: The third dimension of power is shaping ideas so a way of doing things seems best or only - ideology.

rows.prompt: 'There should be very few rules, only to keep people safe' is closest to the view of:
rows.explanation: Nozick's minimal state limits the state to law and order, matching the idea of very few rules.

rows.prompt: What is Direct Provision?
options: Cash payments given to all new migrants
Basic food and shelter for asylum seekers while claims are processed
Social housing for Irish families on low incomes
rows.explanation: Direct Provision meets basic needs of shelter and food rather than providing cash payments.

rows.prompt: A person who leaves their country purely for financial reasons is called:
rows.explanation: Economic migrants have not fled persecution so do not qualify for refugee status.

rows.prompt: A person with no legal bond of nationality with any state is:
rows.explanation: A stateless person has no nationality under national laws.

rows.prompt: Which statement about asylum seekers and refugees is correct?
options: Every asylum seeker becomes a refugee
Every refugee is first an asylum seeker
Asylum seekers have already been granted status
rows.explanation: Not every asylum seeker is recognised as a refugee, but every refugee starts as an asylum seeker.

rows.prompt: When refugees are moved from the country they sought refuge in to another state that agrees to take them, this is:
rows.explanation: Resettlement usually brings long-term residence rights and a chance of citizenship.

rows.prompt: On what date did Direct Provision begin?
rows.explanation: Direct Provision began on 10 April 2000, having been introduced in 1999.

rows.prompt: What weekly allowance did an adult in Direct Provision receive?
rows.explanation: Adults received €38.80 and children €29.80 per week.

rows.prompt: How many regional Direct Provision Centres are mentioned in the chapter?
rows.explanation: After a Dublin reception centre, asylum seekers are assigned to one of 47 regional centres.

rows.prompt: How long after applying can an asylum seeker apply to access the job market?
rows.explanation: They may apply for access to employment nine months after lodging their application.

rows.prompt: Direct Provision was first set up mainly for people escaping:
rows.explanation: It began as an emergency short-term measure, mostly for those fleeing the Balkan war.

rows.prompt: How much did the Irish State spend on Direct Provision in 2020?
rows.explanation: In 2020 the State spent more than €175 million, with costs rising.

rows.prompt: What did the 2017 McMahon Report find?
options: Accommodation was not up to standard
All residents had the right to work
rows.explanation: The report found poor accommodation standards, leading to spending on upgrades and higher costs.

rows.explanation: The average stay is 24 months, though some residents stay up to 12 years.

rows.prompt: Children born into Direct Provision make up what share of residents?
rows.explanation: Children born into the system are 30% of residents, and long-term effects are unknown.

rows.prompt: What is the criticism of inspections in Direct Provision centres?

They focus only on food prices
They ignore residents' emotional and social needs
They happen only once every 12 years

rows.explanation: The Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth published it in February 2021.

rows.prompt: In Phase One of the White Paper, how long would asylum seekers stay in a state-owned centre?
rows.explanation: Phase One is a four-month stay in one of six state-owned centres with an orientation programme.

rows.prompt: Which is part of Phase Two of the White Paper plan?
options: A four-month stay in a state centre
Setting up a bank account on arrival
Own-door apartments or houses in the community
rows.explanation: Phase Two gives self-contained accommodation in the community, plus income and employment supports.

options: Raise the threshold to 40% and extend to other elections
Apply quotas only to the Seanad

options: Young women can see women in government
Women's work may be branded tokenistic
They increase the number of women elected
They are a temporary fix for patriarchy

rows.prompt: Which Kerry family is linked in the chapter to Parish-Pump Politics?
rows.explanation: The chapter lists the dominance of the Healy-Rae family in Kerry as an example.

rows.prompt: Which group is named as excluded from representation because they cannot vote?

rows.prompt: State three key arguments concerning representation from the chapter.
rows.model_answer: Those with the most power can make rules that suit their own interests. Rules protect weaker members of the community from stronger members. Those with most knowledge and wisdom should play the strongest role in making rules; and there is a danger of those in power enforcing rules arbitrarily.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between a refugee and an economic migrant.
rows.model_answer: A refugee has fled their country and cannot or will not return because of fear of persecution due to nationality, religion, race or membership of a social or political group. An economic migrant has chosen to leave purely for financial reasons to find a better life. Economic migrants do not qualify for refugee status or international protection.

rows.prompt: Describe what an asylum seeker receives in Direct Provision.
rows.model_answer: They get a place in one of 47 regional centres after a Dublin reception centre, three meals a day, somewhere to sleep and a weekly allowance of €38.80 per adult and €29.80 per child. They get help with clothing and emergencies and free medical care. Children aged 4-16 attend local schools, and they can apply to work after nine months.

rows.prompt: Outline three problems with the Direct Provision system.
rows.model_answer: Most residents have no access to employment (no right to work until February 2018). Families often share a single room with no cooking facilities, and inspections ignore emotional and social needs. The average stay is 24 months, with some people there up to 12 years, and children born into it make up 30% of residents.

rows.prompt: Describe the two phases in the 2021 White Paper on ending Direct Provision.
rows.model_answer: In Phase One, asylum seekers spend four months in one of six state-owned centres with an orientation programme, English classes, bank accounts, early access to legal aid and healthcare and a daily allowance. In Phase Two they move to own-door apartments or houses in the community with access to education, health, income support, child support and employment, with NGOs supporting vulnerable people.

rows.prompt: Explain what the Citizens' Assembly is and how it works.
rows.model_answer: It is a randomly selected group of citizens, chosen from the electoral register to reflect society by gender, age, region and social class. It discusses important issues, accepts submissions, votes on draft recommendations and reports to the Oireachtas. The Government then responds and arranges debates.

rows.prompt: Give one argument for and one argument against gender quotas.
rows.model_answer: For: quotas increase the number of women elected, from 16% in 2011 to 22% in 2016, giving more representation. Against: they may cause 'indirect discrimination', where a better man loses out so the quota is filled, and women's work may be seen as tokenistic.

rows.prompt: Name four topics you could use to judge whether the Irish electoral system is representative.
rows.model_answer: PRSTV compared with first-past-the-post and D'Hondt; Parish-Pump Politics such as the Healy-Rae family in Kerry; the effectiveness of the Seanad and the President as a check and balance; the Citizens' Assembly; women's representation; and minority groups such as Travellers, LGBTQ+ people, people in Direct Provision and under-18s.

rows.prompt: Describe one argument for and one argument against gender quotas as a means of increasing women's representation in positions of power. (5 marks)
rows.model_answer: For: gender quotas increase the number of women elected; after the 2012 law requiring 30% female candidates, women TDs rose from 16% in 2011 to 22% in 2016. Against: quotas may cause indirect discrimination, where a better candidate loses out to fill the quota, and women may be seen as tokenistic.
rows.marking_scheme: Argument for, described: 3 marks (1 statement + 2 explanation/evidence). Argument against, described: 2 marks. Accept: more women elected, role models for young women, temporary fix for patriarchy; indirect discrimination, tokenism, equal opportunity already exists.

rows.prompt:
Study the information below and answer the question.

'In 2012, the Oireachtas adopted a law requiring parties to have at least 30% female candidates. Women elected rose from 16% in 2011 to 22% in 2016. By 2020 it was 22.5%, placing Ireland 98th in the world for women's representation in national parliaments.'

(i) What does this data show about the effect of gender quotas? (ii) Suggest one further measure to increase women's representation. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: (i) The data shows the quota had a clear early effect: women elected rose by 6 percentage points, from 16% to 22%, between 2011 and 2016. However, progress then stalled, rising only to 22.5% by 2020, which is still well below the 30% candidate quota, and Ireland ranked only 98th in the world, behind Iraq and China. So quotas helped but have not achieved equal representation. (ii) The 2021 Citizens' Assembly recommended raising the quota threshold to 40% for both men and women, extending quotas to European, Seanad and local elections, and increasing penalties for parties that miss the quota.
rows.marking_scheme: (i) 3 points x 2 marks, each using the data: rise 16% to 22%; stall at 22.5% by 2020; still below 30%; 98th in world, behind Iraq and China. (ii) One measure stated and explained: 4 marks (2+2), e.g. 40% threshold, extend to other elections, higher penalties, supports for women furthest from power (National Women's Council).

rows.prompt: Explain two ways in which the Direct Provision system has been criticised. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: First, Direct Provision was meant to be a short-term emergency measure for people fleeing the Balkan war, but it became long-term. The average stay is 24 months and some residents stay up to 12 years, which residents say infringes their human rights. Second, living conditions are poor and limit people's choices. Families often share a single room with no cooking facilities, centres are in B&Bs, hostels and caravan parks, and the 2017 McMahon Report found accommodation not up to standard. Most residents also have no access to work, and inspections ignore emotional and social needs.
rows.marking_scheme: 2 criticisms x 5 marks (2 marks statement + 3 marks explanation with evidence from the chapter). Accept: length of stay, poor accommodation, lack of employment, limited education, 30% children, inspections ignore social/emotional needs, for-profit private contractors, rising cost (over €175m in 2020).

rows.prompt: 'The Irish system of government is effective in representing the will of all the Irish people.' Discuss. (40 marks)
rows.model_answer:
I partly disagree with this statement. Ireland's indirect democracy and PRSTV give a voice to many groups, but evidence shows some groups are still under-represented.

On the positive side, the Citizens' Assembly amplifies the voice of ordinary people. Members are chosen at random from the electoral register to reflect gender, age, region and social class, and recommendations go to the Oireachtas, as with the 2021 assembly on gender equality and the 2023 assembly on drug use. Gender quotas have also helped: after the 2012 law, women TDs rose from 16% in 2011 to 22% in 2016.

However, women are still under-represented. In 2020 only 22.5% of TDs were women and Ireland was 98th in the world, behind Iraq and China. The National Women's Council says women furthest from power, such as Traveller and disabled women, feel policy most. Other groups lack a voice: under-18s cannot vote, and people in Direct Provision, 30% of whom are children, have little say over a system where families share a single room and stay an average of 24 months. This fits the argument that those with power make rules that suit their own interests.

Karl Marx would argue the system serves the privileged, and the chapter asks whether our electoral system is elitist. Robert Nozick, by contrast, would say a minimal state with few rules protects freedom and that quotas are unfair, a view shared by those who say quotas cause indirect discrimination.

Overall, the system represents the majority fairly well but not all Irish people, so reforms such as a 40% quota and better inclusion of minorities are needed.
rows.marking_scheme: Marked for: clear position stated and sustained (8 marks); use of named thinkers/ideas, e.g. Marx, Nozick, Rawls, key arguments on power (10 marks); evidence from the chapter, e.g. gender quota data, Citizens' Assembly, Direct Provision figures, under-18s, National Women's Council (14 marks); counter-argument and conclusion (8 marks).
